proof:
# Strictness and equality in parity mass expansion

Let E be a compact convex subset of R^n times R^d, d>=1, with positive
finite mixed d-volume M. Fix one parity class with positive mass M_r and
largest fiber volume a>0. Then

    M >= 2 M_r-a.                                    (1)

The preceding arithmetic peak-Bonnesen theorem proves (1). This note
gives an explicit strictness term and classifies equality for an ACTUAL
convex E. The same statements apply to any closed cap E=C intersect H.
They do not show that an OC extremizer attains equality in (1).

## 1. A strict term when the class has unequal positive volumes

Suppose the class has a positive fiber volume below a, and let b be
the largest such volume. Then

    M >= 2 M_r-a + [((a^(1/d)+b^(1/d))/2)^d-b].       (2)

The term in brackets is strictly positive.

Let Q consist of the bases in this parity class whose fibers have
volume a, and let p have volume b. Then p is outside conv(Q). Otherwise
an anchored convex representation of p by Q, together with ordinary
Brunn--Minkowski, would put a set of volume at least a in its fiber,
contradicting b<a. Choose a linear functional separating p strictly
from conv(Q), and choose q in Q maximizing this functional on Q.
The integer midpoint (p+q)/2 lies strictly outside conv(Q). Its fiber
has volume at least

    c=((a^(1/d)+b^(1/d))/2)^d>b.

For every volume threshold t in (b,c), the class fibers of volume
greater than t are exactly Q. Their pairwise midpoints are inside
conv(Q) and supply at least2|Q|-1 distinct output bases above threshold
t. The additional midpoint (p+q)/2 is outside that hull and is another
output above t. Thus on this interval the layer-count lower bound used
in (1) improves by at least one. Integrating over (b,c) proves (2).
At all other positive thresholds the original count remains valid.

## 2. Equality forces a one-dimensional equal-volume chain

Assume M=2M_r-a. Section1 forces every positive fiber in the parity
class to have the same volume a. Write their base set P_r, its size N,
and its affine dimension s. If N=1, equality says M=a, so this is the
only positive-volume fiber of E. This case is finished.

For N>=2, the dimension-stratified lattice-dilation inequality in
`candidate 57e3e17a84fce5c1` gives

    M >= [(s+1)N-s(s+1)/2]a.

Its excess over (2N-1)a is

    (s-1)(N-(s+2)/2)a.

Since N>=s+1, this is strictly positive for s>=2. Therefore s=1.

The set P_r contains EVERY point of its residue lattice on its segment
hull: interpolation of endpoint fibers gives volume at least a there.
Let v be the primitive integer vector along this line, directed from
the first to the last base. Because the endpoints are in one parity
class, for an integer L>=1 they are p_0 and p_0+2L v. The points of
the residue class on their segment are exactly p_0+2j v, 0<=j<=L.
Thus N=L+1.

Every integer point p_0+j v, 0<=j<=2L, has a fiber of volume at least
a, by convex interpolation of the extreme fibers. These2L+1=2N-1
fibers already account for the full mass M=(2N-1)a. Hence each has
volume exactly a, and there are no other positive-volume integer fibers.

Let K_0 and K_(2L) be the two extreme fibers. The middle fiber contains
(K_0+K_(2L))/2, and all three have volume a. Equality in the ordinary
Brunn--Minkowski theorem forces the two extremes to be translates:

    K_(2L)=K_0+w.

For every j, the fiber K_j contains K_0+(j/(2L))w and has the same
volume. Inclusion of full-dimensional compact convex bodies of equal
volume implies equality: any extra point, coned to an interior ball,
would add positive volume. Consequently

    K_j=K_0+(j/(2L))w,             0<=j<=2L.          (3)

This proves the asserted classification of all measured fibers. Extra
integer fibers of zero d-volume, if present on the boundary of E, have
not been removed from the set; they carry no mass in this statement.

## 3. An actual OC point in every equality case

For N=1 use the ordinary centroid of the sole positive fiber; every
containing ambient halfspace has mass at least gamma_d M.

For N>=2, let g_0 be the centroid of K_0 and choose the single point

    y=(p_0+L v, g_0+w/2).

Equation(3) proves y belongs to its actual integer fiber. A continuous
affine shear, linear in the integer coordinates and leaving those
coordinates fixed, turns all the fibers in(3) into one common body K
with centroid zero. Such a shear preserves each fiber volume and all
ambient halfspaces. Equivalently the following argument can be written
directly using(3).

Move a containing halfspace parallel until its boundary passes through
y; this cannot increase its mass. If its continuous normal is nonzero,
the middle fiber contributes at least gamma_d a. In each of the L
pairs of equally distant fibers on opposite sides of the middle base,
the two continuous cutting thresholds relative to the common centroid
are opposite. At least one is nonpositive, so its own fiber contributes
at least gamma_d a by ordinary Grünbaum. Hence the total is at least

    (L+1) gamma_d a=N gamma_d a
           =(N/(2N-1)) gamma_d M > (gamma_d/2) M.    (4)

If the continuous normal is zero, the middle fiber and at least one
fiber of each pair are wholly contained, giving N a, which is stronger.
The pair argument includes the zero integer tilt and all closed-boundary
cases. Here N>=2 forces n>=1, so (4) is strictly above2^(-n)gamma_d M.
For n=0 only the N=1 case is possible.

Thus an actual equality case of (1) satisfies OC, with an explicit
deterministic point. This is a classification of equality in an
auxiliary volume inequality. No argument currently forces a hypothetical
general OC counterexample, or its attained arithmetic minimum, to have
that equality. Strictness of (1) by itself is not a contradiction.
